name: Barbell Deficit Deadlift
summary: A conventional barbell deadlift performed while standing on an elevated platform or weight plate to increase range of motion and leg drive off the floor.

setup: Place a low platform, stable mat, or bumper plate on the floor 1 to 3 inches high.
Position a loaded barbell in front of the platform so it rests directly over the midfoot when standing.
Step onto the platform with feet hip-width apart.
Hinge at the hips and bend your knees deeper than usual to grip the barbell just outside your legs using a double overhand, hook, or mixed grip.
Engage your lats to pull the slack out of the bar, bringing your chest up while maintaining a neutral spine.
steps: Drive through the whole foot, extending knees and hips simultaneously to break the bar off the floor.
Keep the bar tracking close to your shins and thighs throughout the pull.
Lock out at the top by fully extending the hips and knees into a tall, standing position without hyperextending the lower back.
Lower the bar under control by hinging backward at the hips until the plates touch the floor.
instructions.breathing: Take a deep diaphragmatic breath and brace your core tightly before pulling, exhaling after passing lockout or upon returning the bar to the floor.
cues: Keep the bar glued to your legs
Pull the slack before you lift

common_faults.fault: Excessive lumbar rounding caused by trying to compensate for the deeper deficit range of motion.
common_faults.correction: Reduce the platform height to one that matches your active hip mobility, or set the hips slightly lower while bracing hard.

common_faults.fault: Hips shooting up before the chest moves off the floor.
common_faults.correction: Push through the floor with your quads and ensure the shoulders and hips rise at the same rate initially.

common_faults.fault: Letting the barbell drift away from the body.
common_faults.correction: Actively contract the lats to keep the bar in continuous contact with your shins and thighs.

precautions: Keep the platform height modest (typically 1 to 2 inches); deficits exceeding 3 inches usually break spinal mechanics without additional benefit.
Ensure the standing platform is completely stable, slip-resistant, and wide enough for your full foot.
